definition.text: The principle that the shift to a low-carbon economy should treat people fairly and leave no workers, places or countries behind.

facts.text: It emerged in the 1980s from US trade unions protecting workers hit by environmental rules.
Tony Mazzocchi of the Oil, Chemical and Atomic Workers Union proposed a 'Superfund for Workers' to compensate and retrain them, and is believed to have coined the term.
Unions won just transition and decent work language in the Paris Agreement's preamble in 2015.
The IPCC stresses investing in low-emission industries, fair jobs, equitable energy access and economic diversification.
As of 2022, 38% of 170 countries referred to just transition in their short-term climate plans.
The EU's Just Transition mechanism helps fossil fuel-dependent regions move to a greener economy.

definition.text: An asset that has suffered an unexpected or early write-down, loss of value, or conversion into a liability.

facts.text: Stranding is part of the 'creative destruction' of growth and innovation and can carry risks for the whole financial system.
Climate change is expected to sharply increase stranded assets in carbon-intensive industries, with ripple effects through the world economy.
The IEA defines them as investments that stop earning a return before the end of their expected economic life because markets or rules change.
The term matters in financial risk management, to avoid losses once an asset has turned into a liability.

definition.text: The loss of value of assets such as fossil fuel reserves and carbon-intensive plants as climate policy, technology and markets shift.

facts.text: It affects oil, gas and coal companies and industries such as steel, aluminium and cement, and also fossil-exporting countries and workers.
Risk factors include environmental change, new regulations such as carbon pricing, falling clean-tech costs, changing social norms and litigation.
A 2021 study found nearly 60 percent of oil and gas reserves and 90 percent of coal reserves must stay unused for a 50 percent chance of 1.5°C.
A 2026 estimate found early closure of coal plants for a 1.5°C pathway would strand around $842 billion.
Net fossil fuel importers gain economically from switching to clean energy, while exporters face stranded assets.

definition.text: Rules that limit or discourage the extraction of natural resources such as fossil fuels, rather than only their use.

facts.text: It can replace or complement demand-side policy, which alone typically causes carbon leakage.
Bohm (1993) first showed that taking fossil fuel reserves off the market can be a beneficial climate policy.
Hoel (1994) showed the best policy combines demand- and supply-side tools, weighted by where leakage is larger, which depends on price elasticities.
Harstad (2012) showed a coalition can gain by buying and retiring fossil fuel reserves in other countries.
Supply-side treaties may be cheaper and easier to monitor, but major emitters are also major producers, so participation is still hard.
The Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative builds on this idea.

definition.text: A charcoal made by heating biomass with little oxygen, intended for use in soil and other organic uses.

facts.text: It is made by pyrolysis, heating biomass without oxygen, which yields solid biochar, liquid bio-oil and syngas.
In soil it can improve aeration and fertility, reduce nutrient leaching and acidity, and cut greenhouse gas emissions from the soil.
Too much, or the wrong feedstock, can harm soil life, change pH and raise salinity.
Because it is so stable, it can stay in soils for thousands of years, which underlies biochar carbon removal.
Pre-Columbian Amazonians made it by smouldering farm waste, creating soils settlers called terra preta.
It benefits degraded tropical soils more than temperate ones.
A 1–2% share of biochar works best in concrete, cutting emissions from cement.

definition.text: A tropical farming method that chars cleared vegetation into biochar instead of burning it, as an alternative to slash-and-burn.

facts.text: Slash-and-burn leaves only 3% of the plant carbon in the soil, while slash-and-char can keep up to 50%.
Switching worldwide could sequester 0.22 to 0.42 Gt C per year.
Biochar soils stay productive, unlike depleted slash-and-burn fields that push farmers to clear more land.
